verses.text: First of all Chaos, the vast gap, came into being, and then
broad-chested Gaia, Earth, forever the firm seat of all
the immortals who hold the peak of snowy Olympus,
and misty Tartarus in the depths of Earth with her wide paths,
and Eros, Desire, most beautiful among the immortal gods,
who loosens limbs and, in every god and every human,
overpowers the mind and careful judgment within the heart.
From Chaos came Erebus, Darkness, and black Night.
From Night in turn came Aether, the bright upper air, and Day,
whom she conceived and bore after joining with Erebus in love.
First Gaia, Earth, gave birth to one equal to herself in size,
starry Uranus, Sky, to cover her on every side
and be a firm seat forever for the blessed gods.
She bore the tall Mountains, lovely homes for goddesses,
the Nymphs who live among the mountains and their valleys.
She also bore the barren sea, raging with waves,
Pontus, without the pleasures of love. Then
she lay with Sky and bore Oceanus with his deep whirlpools,
and Coeus, Crius, Hyperion, and Iapetus,
and Theia, Rhea, Themis, and Mnemosyne,
and Phoebe with her golden crown, and lovely Tethys.
After them the youngest was born, Cronus with his crooked schemes,
the most fearsome of her children. He hated his vigorous father.
Earth also bore the Cyclopes, with their fierce hearts,
Brontes, Steropes, and mighty-hearted Arges,
who gave Zeus his thunder and made his thunderbolt.
In every other way they were like the gods,
but a single eye lay in the middle of each forehead.
They were named Cyclopes, meaning Round-eyes, because
a single round eye lay in each one's forehead.
Strength, force, and skill showed in everything they made.
Then Earth and Sky had three more children,
huge and powerful, too terrible to name,
Cottus, Briareus, and Gyges, towering sons.
A hundred hands sprang from the shoulders of each,
monstrous hands, and each had fifty heads
growing from his shoulders above his sturdy limbs.
Their huge bodies held boundless, mighty strength.
For all the children born to Earth and Sky
were the most fearsome of children, and their father hated them
from the start. As soon as each was born,
he hid them all away and let none come into the light,
deep in a hollow inside Earth. He delighted in this cruel work,
did Sky, while huge Earth groaned within,
cramped by the burden, and thought up a cunning, harmful plan.
Quickly she created gray adamant, a substance of great hardness,
and made a great sickle, then explained her plan to her dear children.
With an aching heart, she spoke to give them courage:
“Children of mine and of a reckless father, if you are willing
to listen to me, we could make your father pay for his cruel abuse.
He was the first to plot these shameful deeds.”
So she spoke. Fear seized them all, and none of them
said a word. But great Cronus, with his crooked schemes, took courage
and answered his loving mother:
“Mother, I promise I can carry out this
deed, for I care nothing for our father
with his shameful name. He was the first to plot these shameful deeds.”
So he spoke, and huge Earth's heart filled with joy.

uncertainties: Verse 118 is marked for deletion in the supplied Greek. It is translated here because it is an assigned verse; including it makes the immortals, rather than all things, the occupants of Earth's firm seat.
